title: Assessing and Gathering Insights into the Feasibility and Acceptability of a Digital Pain Self-Reporting Tool Among People Living with Chronic Musculoskeletal Pain in Pakistan: A Mixed Methods Study
content: Background: Digital pain self-reporting may support longitudinal assessment of chronic pain, but evidence from lower- and middle-income settings is limited. We assessed the feasibility and acceptability of a digital self-reporting pain tool among people living with chronic musculoskeletal pain in Pakistan and gathered users’ insights into the tools’ feasibility and acceptability. Methods: This mixed-methods feasibility study asked participants to use an Android pain self-reporting app over 40 days. Feasibility was assessed using completion rates and predefined engagement thresholds. Acceptability was assessed using an end-of-study questionnaire. Two in-person focus groups were conducted, which were analysed using framework analysis, and qualitative findings were analysed descriptively and integrated for the final presentation. Results: Sixty-two participants submitted at least one pain report, generating a total of 945 reports.  Participants reported a mean of 9.7 ± 11 of 40 study days, equivalent to a mean completion rate of 24.0% ± 28.6%. Eleven participants (18%) reported for at least seven consecutive days, 11 (18%) submitted at least two reports per week, and four (6.5%) submitted at least four reports per week throughout six weeks. Twenty-nine participants (47%) completed the acceptability questionnaire. Most respondents found the app useful (26/29, 90%), easy for indicating pain location (28/29, 97%) and selecting pain intensity (25/29, 86%). Technical issues such as connectivity were common barriers, alongside forgetting to self-report. Focus group discussions with participants attending follow up consultations reported that the app helped them communicate their pain more accurately and enabled developing greater awareness of their pain. However, additional guidance on using the app and pain self-management approaches could be useful. Conclusions: Though a digital pain self-reporting tool is acceptable in low-resource settings, its long-term feasibility remains constrained by low user engagement, which is driven by personal, social and technological and utility related aspects. Future research should explore how improving these aspects can improve outcomes across diverse population subgroups.
